Redefining Airway Management in Maxillofacial Trauma: 
The Strategic Implementation of Sub-Mental Intubation
Rahul Kumar Chaudhary1 | Sajjad Ahmed Khan2 | Prajwal Raj Bista1 | Lalit Kumar Rajbanshi1
1Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care, Birat Medical College Teaching Hospital, Morang, Nepal | 2Pediatric Surgery, Birat Medical College 
Teaching Hospital, Morang, Nepal
Correspondence: Rahul Kumar Chaudhary (rahulkr9991@gmail.com)
Received: 17 August 2024 | Revised: 29 September 2024 | Accepted: 25 October 2024
Funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.
Keywords: airway management | facial fractures | Le Fort fractures | maxillofacial trauma | sub-mental intubation | trauma surgery
ABSTRACT
Submental intubation offers a valuable alternative for managing airway in patients with complex maxillofacial injuries, providing unobstructed access for surgical intervention and reducing complications associated with traditional intubation methods. It 
enhances both surgical visibility and patient safety.
JEL Classification: Anesthesia
1|Introduction
Maxillofacial trauma resulting from motor vehicle collisions 
often presents significant challenges in airway management 
and surgical intervention due to the complexity of the injuries 
involved. The management of the airway in such cases is crucial, as traditional intubation methods may be complicated by 
facial deformities and impaired mouth opening. One innovative 
technique that has proven valuable in such scenarios is submental intubation.
Submental intubation involves placing an endotracheal tube 
through a small incision made in the submental area, providing 
an alternative airway access when conventional methods are not 
feasible [1]. This technique has been particularly beneficial in 
cases with severe facial trauma, such as Le Fort fractures, where 
conventional oral or nasal intubation methods are compromised

by significant swelling, fractures, or deformities [2]. The effectiveness of submental intubation in managing complex maxillofacial injuries has been well-documented. Studies indicate that 
it provides a clear and stable airway while avoiding complications associated with other intubation techniques [3]. This approach facilitates unobstructed access to the oral cavity, which 
is essential for performing comprehensive facial reconstructive 
surgeries. Additionally, submental intubation reduces the risk of 
dental injury and enhances surgical visibility [4].
This case presentation details the use of submental intubation 
in a patient with extensive maxillofacial injuries resulting from 
a motor vehicle collision. The patient exhibited a Le Fort II fracture, a frontal bone fracture, and a right frontotemporal contusion, which complicated conventional airway management. The 
successful application of submental intubation in this scenario 
underscores its value as a viable technique in specific clinical 
situations.
2|Case Presentation
2.1|Case History/Examination
A 32-year-old male was admitted to the trauma unit following a 
severe motor vehicle collision. The accident resulted in extensive 
maxillofacial injuries that complicated both his airway management and overall treatment approach. Upon presentation, 
the patient exhibited significant facial swelling, nasal bleeding,

and multiple bruises on the forehead and face. The swelling and 
trauma had severely restricted mouth opening, making conventional intubation techniques difficult and potentially hazardous. 
A thorough physical examination revealed notable facial deformities and significant swelling, which further complicated the 
assessment of his airway.
CT imaging was conducted to assess the full extent of the injuries. The results demonstrated a Le Fort II fracture, which 
involves the midface including the maxilla, nasal bones, and

inferior orbital rims. Additionally, the imaging revealed a 
frontal bone fracture and a right frontotemporal contusion, 
suggesting possible intracranial involvement. These injuries 
posed substantial risks, including potential airway obstruction and complications that could affect the surgical intervention needed.
3|Methods (Differential Diagnosis, 
Investigations, and Treatment)
In managing this patient, differential diagnoses included potential airway obstruction due to the extensive facial injuries, as well 
as the risk of additional undiagnosed fractures or internal injuries. The presence of the frontotemporal contusion raised concerns about possible intracranial damage, which could further 
complicate airway management and overall surgical strategy.
The diagnostic approach was comprehensive. CT scans were 
crucial in evaluating the extent of the facial fractures and potential intracranial injuries. Preoperative assessments included 
standard laboratory tests to check for anemia, coagulopathy, 
and overall health status. Although the CT scans provided initial insights, further neuroimaging might have been considered 
if there was a suspicion of more extensive intracranial injury. 
Additionally, a detailed airway assessment was planned, which 
might have included fiberoptic evaluation, given the restricted 
mouth opening.
Given the complexity of the patient's injuries and the challenges 
associated with conventional intubation, submental intubation 
was chosen as the most appropriate method for securing the airway. The patient was positioned supine on the operating table, 
with standard monitoring applied, including continuous pulse 
oximetry, ECG, and non-invasive blood pressure monitoring. 
Sedation was carefully induced to ensure patient comfort while 
maintaining hemodynamic stability. Preoxygenation with 100% 
oxygen was administered to optimize the patient's oxygen reserves prior to intubation.
The surgical team performed a submental incision, approximately 1.5 cm in length, in the submental region to facilitate the creation of a tunnel through the submental space 
(Figure  1). This approach allowed for the endotracheal tube 
to be guided through the tunnel, bypassing the difficulties 
presented by the facial injuries. The incision was followed

by blunt dissection to avoid damaging vital structures in the 
area. The endotracheal tube was initially inserted orally and 
positioned in the trachea. Once correct placement was confirmed via auscultation and capnography, the tube was withdrawn from the oral cavity and guided through the submental 
tunnel, where it was secured externally to ensure stability and 
effective ventilation.
Intraoperatively, intermaxillary fixation was employed to maintain adequate dental occlusion before the fixation of fractures. 
During the surgical procedure, general anesthesia was maintained with a combination of inhalational agents and intravenous 
opioids. This approach was chosen to ensure stable hemodynamics and adequate analgesia throughout the operation. The submental intubation allowed for unobstructed access to the oral 
cavity, which was crucial for the extensive reconstructive surgery 
required. The surgical intervention included stabilization of the 
Le Fort II fracture and repair of the frontal bone fracture, using 
plates and screws to align and secure the fractured segments.
Throughout the operation, the patient remained hemodynamically stable, with continuous monitoring ensuring that any 
fluctuations in vital signs were promptly managed. The surgical team was able to complete the necessary reconstructive procedures without complications, thanks to the effective airway 
management provided by the submental intubation.
4|Results (Treatment and Follow-Up)
The postoperative course for the patient was favorable. He was 
successfully extubated in the operating room at the end of the 
surgery. The submental incision was closed with sutures, and 
the patient was monitored in the post-anesthesia care unit. 
Follow-up care revealed a satisfactory recovery, with no signs of 
airway obstruction or infection. The submental incision healed 
without complications, and the patient demonstrated positive 
progress during subsequent follow-up visits.
This case highlights the effectiveness of submental intubation 
in managing complex maxillofacial injuries where traditional 
intubation methods are impractical or risky. The technique provided a clear airway management pathway and allowed for unobstructed access to the oral cavity, which was essential for the 
successful completion of the facial reconstructive surgery. The

its value and illustrates the careful considerations necessary for

5|Discussion
Maxillofacial trauma, particularly from severe motor vehicle 
accidents, often presents complex challenges in airway management and surgical intervention. Traditional methods of intubation can be significantly impeded by facial deformities, 
fractures, and swelling, which can complicate both access and 
visualization. In such scenarios, submental intubation offers a 
novel and effective alternative. This case highlights the successful use of submental intubation in a patient with extensive maxillofacial injuries, emphasizing its advantages over conventional 
methods.
Submental intubation, introduced in the 1980s by Hwang et al., 
has become a recognized technique for managing the airway in 
complex facial trauma cases [5]. The technique involves creating 
a small incision in the submental area to establish an airway 
through a tunnel created under the skin. This approach is particularly beneficial in cases where oral or nasal intubation is obstructed by severe facial injuries or where facial surgery requires 
unobstructed access to the oral cavity [6].
This case is notable for its complexity, involving a Le Fort II fracture, frontal bone fracture, and a right frontotemporal contusion. 
The Le Fort II fracture, which affects the midface and can lead to 
significant displacement of facial structures, presents a particular 
challenge for conventional intubation [7]. The frontal bone fracture and associated frontotemporal contusion further complicate 
airway management due to potential intracranial involvement 
and additional facial trauma [8]. In such situations, submental 
intubation provides a critical advantage by bypassing the obstructed oral cavity and allowing for direct access to the airway.
Several studies have supported the efficacy of submental intubation in managing complex maxillofacial injuries. For 
example, Saravanan et  al. conducted a systematic review 
demonstrating that submental intubation is highly effective in

scenarios where traditional intubation methods are compromised due to severe facial trauma [3]. Their review noted that 
submental intubation not only improves surgical access but 
also reduces the risk of further injury to the facial structures 
during intubation.
Comparing this case with similar reported cases, several key 
points emerge. In a study by Hsu et  al., submental intubation 
was utilized successfully in patients with Le Fort fractures and 
other complex facial injuries [2]. Their findings underscore the 
technique's ability to provide stable airway management and 
enhance surgical visibility. Similarly, Nair et  al. reported that 
submental intubation significantly reduces the risk of dental 
damage and improves the overall safety and efficacy of surgical 
procedures in patients with severe facial trauma [1]. These studies align with the experience described in this case, highlighting 
the technique's role in facilitating complex facial reconstructive 
surgeries.
Additionally, Aboh et  al. highlighted that this intubation 
method can be beneficial in managing cases of oral impaction 
related to palatal tumors, showcasing its versatility in various clinical contexts  [9]. Furthermore, Chisci et  al. emphasized the importance of maintaining dental occlusion during 
surgery, as it significantly contributes to the overall success 
of maxillofacial reconstructive procedures [10]. The use of 
submental intubation has been established as a critical technique in trauma care, particularly for cases where traditional 
intubation methods are impractical. This approach allows 
for tailored airway management strategies, optimizing patient outcomes in high-risk situations. Chisci and Hatia also 
highlighted the role of antibiotics in preventing postoperative 
infections in orthognathic surgery, underscoring the need for 
a comprehensive approach to patient care in these complex 
cases [11].
A noteworthy aspect of this case is the use of submental intubation in conjunction with comprehensive facial reconstructive surgery, including stabilization of both the Le Fort II 
fracture and the frontal bone fracture. This approach allowed

for meticulous surgical repair while avoiding the complications associated with other intubation techniques, such as potential obstruction or displacement of the endotracheal tube 
during surgery. The successful outcome of this case further 
supports the utility of submental intubation in similar highrisk situations.
In comparison, traditional methods of intubation often face limitations in such contexts. Orotracheal intubation can be challenging or impossible due to facial swelling, displacement of the 
maxilla, or dental injuries. Nasotracheal intubation is contraindicated in the presence of facial fractures, particularly those 
involving the naso-orbito-ethmoidal complex, due to the risk of 
further injury or infection [12]. Submental intubation effectively 
addresses these limitations by providing an alternative route 
that circumvents the obstructed or compromised oral and nasal 
passages.
This case also underscores the importance of tailored airway 
management strategies in trauma care. The decision to use 
submental intubation was guided by the specific anatomical 
and clinical challenges presented by the patient's injuries. 
This personalized approach is critical for optimizing patient 
outcomes in complex trauma cases and illustrates the adaptability of airway management techniques to individual patient needs.
Maxillofacial trauma often presents complex airway management challenges due to severe injuries. This case highlights the 
advantages of submental intubation over conventional methods, particularly in the context of extensive injuries like Le Fort 
fractures and frontal bone fractures. Previous studies support 
the efficacy of this technique in facilitating stable airway management and surgical visibility, thus reducing the risk of further 
injury. Submental intubation allows performing intermaxillary 
fixation to maintain dental occlusion before fixation with plates 
and screws, ensuring efficacy of the procedure. The use of submental intubation has been established as a critical technique in 
trauma care, particularly for cases where traditional intubation

high-risk situations.
In summary, the successful application of submental intubation 
in this case highlights its significant advantages in managing

complex maxillofacial injuries. The technique not only provides 
a stable and accessible airway but also enhances surgical visibility and reduces the risk of further injury. This case reinforces 
the findings of previous studies and supports the continued use 
of submental intubation as a valuable tool in the management of 
severe facial trauma.
6|Conclusion
Thus, submental intubation proves to be an invaluable technique 
in managing airway challenges associated with complex maxillofacial trauma. This case illustrates the effectiveness of submental intubation in providing a stable and unobstructed airway, 
facilitating comprehensive facial reconstructive surgery in the 
presence of severe injuries such as Le Fort fractures and frontal 
bone fractures. The technique not only addresses the limitations 
of conventional intubation methods but also enhances surgical 
visibility and reduces the risk of further injury. The successful 
outcome of this case aligns with existing literature and underscores the importance of tailored airway management strategies 
in trauma care. Submental intubation should be considered a 
critical option in the toolkit for managing complex facial trauma, 
offering significant advantages in both safety and procedural 
efficacy.
